0.title: Covenant Love and the Gospel
0.essay:
Marriage is not a human invention that God later blessed. It is a divine institution, established in the garden before sin, and officiated at its first wedding by God himself.

Before the fall

Before any shadow of disorder, God said, “It is not good that the man should be alone” (Genesis 2:18). Then he made a woman and brought her to the man. Marriage was God’s idea before humanity had the chance to propose any alternatives.

A mystery revealed

Yet the Bible’s theology of marriage is richer and stranger than even this beginning suggests. In Ephesians 5, Paul calls marriage a mystery, a word he uses for truths hidden in God until the time came to reveal them. The mystery is this: from the very beginning, marriage was designed to be a living drama of the gospel, a sign pointing to the relationship between Christ and his church. Every Christian marriage, whether the couple knows it or not, is a public sermon about the love of Christ for his people.

Exalting and demanding

That is both the most exalting and the most demanding thing that can be said about marriage. It is exalting, because ordinary Christian marriages, with all their imperfections and dailiness, share in something cosmic. It is demanding, because the standard of a Christian marriage is not social convention or personal happiness, but the self-giving, promise-keeping love of Christ for his church.

The chapters

The Foundation: marriage as creation ordinance and gospel sign. Covenant: what makes a marriage a marriage. Husbands: the call to Christlike servant leadership. Wives: the call to gospel-shaped strength. When Marriage Is Hard: conflict, forgiveness and the long road. And Marriage, Singleness, and the Kingdom: both callings honoured.

For reflection

If your marriage, or a marriage you know well, were a sermon about Christ and his church, what would people learn from it?

1.title: The Foundation: Marriage as Creation Ordinance and Gospel Sign
1.essay:
Marriage was established at creation, before the fall, for all humanity and not only for the people of God. It has a design written into creation itself, and that design points to Christ.

Back to the beginning

When Jesus was asked about divorce, he did not start with Moses. He went back past Sinai to creation: “Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female” (Matthew 19:4). The shape of marriage is not negotiable, because it is not a human construction. It is the Creator’s design.

The blueprint

Genesis 2:24 gives that design: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.” Jesus calls this the foundation (Matthew 19:5), and Paul quotes it too (Ephesians 5:31). It repays slow reading.

Leave. This is a decisive transfer of primary loyalty. It need not be geographical; you may live next door to your parents. But the marriage now takes priority over the family you grew up in.

Hold fast. The Hebrew word is used for cleaving to God (Deuteronomy 10:20) and for Ruth clinging to Naomi (Ruth 1:14). It is the language of determined, tenacious faithfulness.

One flesh. This is not only physical union but the joining of two whole lives into one. Together the three describe a bond so total that Jesus concludes, “What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate” (Matthew 19:6).

God joins

Notice whose act this is. Jesus grounds the permanence of marriage not in the couple’s feelings, nor the approval of the state, nor the survival of romance, but in God, who joins two into one. The joining is God’s act; the separating would be man’s. This is not legalism. It protects the most intimate human relationship from a culture that treats marriage as a renewable contract. The permanence of marriage is the security in which one-flesh intimacy can grow.

God as witness

Malachi confronted Israel’s casual divorce with a sobering reminder: “the LORD was witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant” (Malachi 2:14). God was present at your wedding. He heard the vows. A marriage cannot be dissolved simply because one party now finds it inconvenient. And the phrase “wife of your youth” is tender as well as binding: she is the one who shared your beginning and has walked the long road with you.

The purposes of marriage

The Reformers named three purposes of marriage: children and their nurture (Genesis 1:28), the companionship and help of husband and wife (Genesis 2:18), and a remedy against sexual immorality (1 Corinthians 7:2–5). Modern evangelicals have rightly stressed companionship, the deep friendship between husband and wife. Tim Keller adds a fourth, drawn from Ephesians 5: marriage as a means of mutual sanctification, in which each spouse helps the other grow into the likeness of Christ.

Augustine spoke of three goods of marriage: children, faithfulness, and the sacred bond that cannot be broken, a sign of God’s covenant. These shaped the church’s thinking for fifteen centuries. Much of the modern confusion about marriage comes from having abandoned that framework without replacing it with anything as deep.

A gospel sign

Then comes Paul’s astonishing comment. Having quoted Genesis 2:24, he adds, “This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32). The one-flesh union of husband and wife is a sign. Not a weak symbol, but a real, enacted picture of a deeper reality. The marriage covenant points to the covenant between Christ and his people.

This was true from the beginning. Every wedding in history has echoed the story of the divine Bridegroom and his bride. That does not make marriage merely a teaching aid. It makes it glorious, because what it points to is the most glorious reality there is.

A mirror

Keller also observes that marriage holds up a mirror. Its closeness strips away pretence and shows each partner who they really are, not who they imagine themselves to be. That is not a design flaw. It is the design. In the closest human relationship our idols, fears and selfishness are most fully exposed, and so is our need for grace. A couple who understands this will not run from the hard seasons, but will stay in them, trusting that God is at work.

For reflection

Which part of Genesis 2:24 — leaving, holding fast, or becoming one flesh — most needs attention in your own marriage or in how you think about marriage?

2.title: Covenant: What Makes a Marriage a Marriage
2.essay:
The word that defines marriage in Scripture is not love, though love is essential, and not compatibility, though friendship matters greatly. The word is covenant.

What a covenant is

A covenant is a solemn, binding, self-giving promise made before God that creates a relationship. In the biblical world, covenants were often sealed with blood, as if to say: may this happen to me if I break my word. The wedding vow is a covenant oath. It binds the one who makes it, whatever their future feelings or circumstances.

Covenant or contract?

Modern Western culture has largely reduced marriage to an elevated romantic partnership, an arrangement that lasts as long as both find it fulfilling. The test is subjective: are we still happy, still in love, still fulfilled? The biblical test is objective: did we make a covenant, did God witness it, and have we kept it?

The difference is crucial. A contract is an exchange between parties who remain essentially self-interested. I give what I agreed to give and expect what I was promised in return. When the benefit stops, the contract can end. A covenant is different. I give myself, and I commit to the relationship regardless of what I receive. As Michael Horton puts it, a covenant creates a bond between persons that carries moral weight beyond mutual benefit. It creates a “we” that has claims on both partners, however either feels on a given day.

None of this means feelings are unimportant or that unhappy marriages are acceptable. The biblical call is to deep love, real friendship and lasting joy. But feelings are not the foundation. The covenant is the foundation on which feelings are built, protected and sustained. The couple who keeps their promises when the feelings are cold, and does the work of love when love is not easy, has the best hope of warm feelings over the long haul.

The vow creates a marriage

The wedding vow does not merely describe something. It makes something. When a couple say “I will,” a marriage comes into existence that did not exist a moment before. So a marriage is not made by feelings, which come and go, but by a word spoken before God, which stands. The words “in sickness and in health, for better, for worse” are still in force. That is both the burden and the beauty of the covenant.

Steadfast love

The model for this is God’s own covenant love, which the Old Testament calls hesed, his steadfast love. It is not first a feeling but a commitment, the love that keeps showing up whatever the response. Ruth showed it to Naomi: “For where you go I will go” (Ruth 1:16). She went further: “Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried” (Ruth 1:17). Nothing was held back, no exit kept open. That is why these words, though spoken between a woman and her mother-in-law, are so often read at weddings.

Strong as death

The Song of Solomon celebrates the passionate, exclusive love of husband and wife with a frankness that can make readers blush. It reaches its height here: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death” (Song of Solomon 8:6). Death does not let go. Neither does covenant love. And the verse ends by calling love’s flame “the very flame of the LORD” (Song of Solomon 8:6), hinting that married passion is, in some mysterious way, a spark of God’s own love.

Love that bears all things

Paul’s great chapter on love is not romantic poetry. It is a demanding description of faithfulness: “Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7). It covers the other’s failures rather than exposing them, for “love covers all offenses” (Proverbs 10:12). It assumes the best. It does not give up on the other person’s capacity to grow. It stays under pressure instead of escaping. Such love is possible not because we are exceptionally strong, but because the God who commands it supplies it.

Hosea’s marriage

The most demanding command ever given to a husband was given to Hosea. His wife Gomer had been unfaithful, and God said, “Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress, even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods” (Hosea 3:1). Hosea’s marriage became a living parable of God’s love, which pursues the faithless, pays the price of redemption and restores what was broken.

This is not to make light of infidelity or its devastation. But a marriage that has survived betrayal and returned to faithfulness is not a lesser marriage. A couple who knows what forgiveness costs has learned something about the cross that comfortable couples have not.

In sickness and in health

Robertson McQuilkin was president of Columbia Bible College when his wife Muriel began to show signs of Alzheimer’s disease. As her condition worsened, he resigned his post to care for her full-time. She had cared for him sacrificially for decades, he said. But more deeply, he had made a promise. “In sickness and in health” was not a formula he had recited, but a vow made to a person before God. His decision moved thousands, because it made covenant love visible.

For reflection

Do you tend to think of marriage more as a contract or as a covenant? Where in your own life is God calling you to keep a promise when the feelings are not there?

3.title: Husbands: The Call to Christlike Servant Leadership
3.essay:
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). It is the most demanding sentence ever addressed to a husband. The standard is the cross.

The standard is Calvary

The love required of husbands is not romantic affection, not general kindness, not even sacrifice in some vague sense. It is the love that went to Calvary: the love that took on the full weight of another’s need and gave everything for the good of the beloved. The Greek word is agape, the love that chooses the other’s good whatever it costs. It is not what a husband feels when he is attracted to his wife. It is what he does when the feelings are absent and the cost is high. It is commanded, because it rests not on emotion but on covenant and character.

Neither tyrant nor bystander

This sets the husband’s calling apart from two errors. One is the authoritarian husband, who rules his home and expects to be served. The other treats husband and wife as interchangeable partners with no distinct responsibilities. The New Testament calls for headship (Ephesians 5:23): real, responsible leadership. But it is a headship shaped entirely by the Servant-King who washed feet and died on a cross. Authority exercised as Christ exercised his always looks, to an onlooker, less like power and more like sacrifice.

Servant leadership

Jesus said, “For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45), and “The greatest among you shall be your servant” (Matthew 23:11). This is not merely good advice. It is the shape of authority in the kingdom, modelled by the King.

A husband who leads by serving takes out the rubbish, gets up with the baby, sits with his wife in her grief, and carries the weight of the household’s needs without making her feel guilty for having needs. That is not weakness. It is the power of the cross, applied at home. The question that marks true headship is not “What am I owed?” but “What can I give?” Complementarian writers such as Wayne Grudem stress that headship is not oppression but responsibility: the husband answers to God for how he leads his home.

Love that aims at her flourishing

Ephesians tells us what Christ’s love aims at: “that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor” (Ephesians 5:26–27). A husband’s love has the same goal. Not his own comfort or status, but her flourishing, spiritually, emotionally, physically and relationally.

The picture of a gardener helps. A gardener’s job is not to be the most beautiful plant, but to tend the garden so that everything in it thrives. A husband who prays for his wife, encourages her gifts, gives her security so she can take risks, and speaks words that build rather than diminish, is loving as Ephesians commands. The test is not “Does she serve me?” but “Am I serving her?”

Understanding and honour

Peter adds two more things: “Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered” (1 Peter 3:7). To live “in an understanding way” means to pay real attention to who she is: her needs, fears, gifts and experiences, not the wife he imagines. And she is to be honoured as a fellow heir of grace, his equal in dignity before God.

Then comes the warning. A husband who dishonours his wife will find his prayers hindered. He cannot treat her with contempt at home and then lift up holy hands on Sunday. The health of his walk with God is bound up with the health of his marriage. God notices.

Joy, not only duty

Scripture does not only call husbands to sacrifice and endurance. It calls them to joy: “rejoice in the wife of your youth” (Proverbs 5:18). The surrounding verses use some of the most intimate language in the Old Testament to describe a husband’s delight in his wife. A husband who has reduced his marriage to duty has not yet arrived at what Proverbs envisions. Covenant and delight are not rivals. The covenant is the safe place where delight can grow.

Eros and charity

C. S. Lewis, in The Four Loves, observes that romantic love does not guarantee self-giving love. Romance can be very self-focused, wanting the beloved mainly for the feelings they produce. Charity chooses the beloved’s good. A marriage that begins with romance but never grows charity will eventually run dry, because romance rises and falls with age and circumstance. A marriage that adds charity to romance has a foundation that holds.

An impossible standard

No husband can love like this in his own strength. That is the point. The call to love as Christ loved drives a man to his knees, to the cross and to the Spirit. A husband who takes Ephesians 5:25 seriously will spend his whole marriage discovering how far short he falls and how much he needs grace. That is not despair. It is the doorway to the marriage God intends.

For reflection

Husbands: what would it look like this week to ask “What can I give?” rather than “What am I owed?” Where is God calling you to serve your wife in a way that costs you something?

4.title: Wives: The Call to Gospel-Shaped Strength
4.essay:
“Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:22). Few verses in the New Testament are so misunderstood, misapplied and therefore feared. Read in context, it describes not weakness but a dignified, gospel-shaped strength.

Abused and avoided

This verse has been used to justify abuse, to silence gifted women and to enforce a harsh patriarchy that the text itself does not support. And it has been dismissed or explained away by those who rightly recoil from such abuses, but who have abandoned the text instead of recovering it. Both responses miss what Paul actually says.

Context is everything

Ephesians 5:22 cannot be read without the verse before it, “submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ” (Ephesians 5:21), or the verses after it, where husbands are called to die for their wives (Ephesians 5:25–33). The submission Paul describes is not that of a slave to a master or a soldier to a general. It is the free, willing, intelligent response of a wife to a husband who is himself called to lay down his life for her.

The pattern is the church and Christ: “Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands” (Ephesians 5:24). The church does not submit to Christ because it is forced to, but because he is worthy and his leadership is trustworthy. He gave himself for her good. So the wife’s submission is not blind obedience. It is the glad trust a redeemed person gives to a servant-leader whose authority answers to the cross. And it never means following a husband into sin, or staying in danger. Her first loyalty is to the Lord.

What submission means

The New Testament uses the same word for Christ’s submission to the Father (1 Corinthians 15:28), Christians’ submission to governing authorities (Romans 13:1), and church members’ submission to their leaders (Hebrews 13:17). In every case it is voluntary and purposeful, and it sits alongside full dignity and equality of person. A wife’s submission is an act of trust in God’s order, not an admission of inferiority.

Some complementarian writers have argued that this order mirrors an eternal order within the Trinity. Others, wary of implying any inequality within God, ground it instead in creation (1 Corinthians 11:8–9; 1 Timothy 2:13) and in the Son’s willing submission to the Father in his saving mission. The second is the safer ground.

Equal heirs

Paul also wrote, “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). All discussion of roles must rest on that. A wife is not less than her husband. She is a fellow heir of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7), equally precious to God, equally redeemed, equally indwelt by the Spirit. Different roles do not mean different worth, just as the Son’s willing submission in his mission does not make him less than the Father. Egalitarian and complementarian Christians both affirm Galatians 3:28. They disagree about what it implies for roles in marriage and ministry.

Strength and dignity

The woman of Proverbs 31 is not a picture of passive domesticity. She manages a household, runs a business, cares for the poor, speaks wisdom and is praised at the city gates. “Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come. She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue” (Proverbs 31:25–26). Her wisdom is not silent. Her kindness is active.

The source of her fearlessness comes at the end: “Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised” (Proverbs 31:30). She has placed her security in God, and that frees her from anxious grasping.

This chapter has been both over-applied, as a checklist that crushes real women under impossible expectations, and under-appreciated, as an ancient domestic ideal. Read carefully, it is a portrait of character, not a job description. She is the Bible’s answer to both the doormat and the superwoman.

The hidden person of the heart

Peter writes, “Do not let your adorning be external,” but rather “let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God’s sight is very precious” (1 Peter 3:3–4). He is not banning jewellery. He is redirecting attention from outward to inward beauty.

The word gentle is the same word used of Jesus (Matthew 11:29) and of the meek who inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5). It is not timidity but strength under control, power in the service of love. Quiet describes a settled, unagitated spirit: not silence, but peace. Such beauty does not fade, and God himself treasures it.

The strength of surrender

Elisabeth Elliot lost her husband Jim when he was killed by the Waorani people he had gone to reach. She then went to live among those who had killed him. She wrote powerfully about surrender, not as weakness but as the deepest kind of strength: the way up is down, the way to life is through death. Her life embodied what she taught, and it was a life of remarkable influence.

Together, a picture of the gospel

What is most remarkable about the wife’s calling in Ephesians 5 is its dignity. The church’s response to Christ does not diminish the church; it is her glory. A wife who responds to her husband’s servant leadership with grace, wisdom and willing partnership is not less than he is. Together they act out the gospel: the one who leads by sacrifice, and the one who responds with glad and free trust.

For reflection

Wives: how does seeing submission in the light of Christ and the church change how you hear Ephesians 5:22? Where do you most need the fearless trust of the woman who “laughs at the time to come”?

5.title: When Marriage Is Hard: Conflict, Forgiveness, and the Long Road
5.essay:
No couple stands at the altar expecting their marriage to be hard. Yet most marriages, at some point, are. The Bible is utterly realistic about this, and the gospel is the resource for it.

The romantic myth

One of the most destructive ideas in modern marriage is the belief that love should feel effortless, and that difficulty means something is fundamentally wrong. It teaches couples to read conflict as incompatibility and hardship as proof that they married the wrong person. In reality, conflict is the normal terrain of two sinners learning to live as one.

Tim Keller calls romantic love one of the great idols of the modern West. When romantic feeling becomes the foundation of a marriage, the marriage is only as secure as the feeling, and feelings rise and fall with health, stress, tiredness and the thousand pressures of shared life. A marriage built on covenant has a foundation that holds when the feeling is cold. And often the feelings return, because love is not only a feeling but a practice, and practised love produces felt love.

Scripture’s realism

The Bible does not pretend. Proverbs is blunt: “It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife” (Proverbs 21:9). It knows the spouse who forsakes the covenant (Proverbs 2:16–17). Even the Song of Solomon includes seasons of separation and anxious longing (Song of Solomon 3:1–4). And Paul says plainly that “those who marry will have worldly troubles” (1 Corinthians 7:28). Not might. Will. He says this not to put anyone off marriage, but to prepare them for it. Those who expect trouble, and understand it as the place where God sanctifies and gives grace, will not be thrown when it comes.

Catch it early

Proverbs is brilliantly practical about conflict: “The beginning of strife is like letting out water, so quit before the quarrel breaks out” (Proverbs 17:14). The first sharp tone, the first accusing word, is like the first leak in a dam. At that moment the flood can still be stopped. Wise couples learn to notice when a conversation is tipping into a fight, and have the humility to ask, “Is this really worth fighting about?”

Hardness of heart

When asked about divorce, Jesus said, “Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so” (Matthew 19:8). That makes the hard seasons a spiritual diagnostic. The desire to escape the covenant is not only a reaction to difficult circumstances. It can be a sign of a heart growing hard towards the person we promised to love.

This is not a word against the abandoned or the abused. They are not the ones with hard hearts. It is a warning to the spouse who finds the other inconvenient and has let the heart calcify. And the remedy is not stronger willpower, but the God who promises, “I will give you a new heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).

Forgiving as God forgave

Paul writes, “Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). Kind. Tenderhearted, which is the opposite of the hardness Jesus warned about. Forgiving. And the engine of it all is “as God in Christ forgave you.”

God’s forgiveness is the model: complete, costly, and not earned. It is also the motive: those who have received such mercy cannot withhold it from their spouse. A couple who forgives regularly and genuinely, who does not keep accounts or use past failures as weapons, is a couple in whom the gospel is bearing fruit at the most intimate level.

When divorce is permitted

Jesus permits divorce in cases of sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9). Paul permits it when an unbelieving spouse abandons the marriage: “if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so” (1 Corinthians 7:15). A spouse who leaves to escape abuse is not committing the separation Paul forbids. Safety comes first, abuse must be reported, and many Reformed pastors and church courts treat persistent, unrepentant abuse as a form of desertion. The study on Divorce and Remarriage treats these questions more fully.

These are permissions, not commands. The direction of the gospel is always towards restoration where that is possible and safe. But a pastor who refuses to recognise any legitimate ground for divorce adds a burden Scripture does not impose.

Holy more than happy

Gary Thomas, in Sacred Marriage, asks a provocative question: what if God designed marriage to make us holy more than to make us happy? That is not a call to resigned misery. It is a recovery of the biblical vision. The very things that make marriage hard — living with someone who sees you clearly, who has needs you cannot meet, who sins against you and is sinned against — are the things that drive you to the gospel.

The couple who stayed

One of the strongest testimonies to the gospel is the couple who stayed. They endured the hard season, kept forgiving when it was costly, and chose the covenant when feeling argued for leaving. They came out the other side with a marriage deeper, more honest and more grounded than anything the honeymoon produced. Such couples are not in the magazines. But they are in your church, and their stories are worth telling. Hard marriages are not failed marriages. Often they are the marriages where the gospel is most visibly at work.

For reflection

Where does conflict usually begin in your marriage, or in your closest relationships? What would it look like to “quit before the quarrel breaks out,” and to forgive as God in Christ forgave you?

6.title: Marriage, Singleness, and the Kingdom
6.essay:
The church has often treated marriage as the normal Christian life and singleness as a problem to be solved. The New Testament holds both callings in honour, and points both to a greater wedding.

The two greatest were single

Jesus never married. Paul was unmarried, or perhaps widowed, by the time of his letters. The Son of God and the apostle to the Gentiles both lived single lives. That should give the church pause before treating unmarried adults with pity or puzzlement. A single person is not incomplete, waiting for marriage to finish them. They are complete in Christ, with a particular freedom to give themselves to the work of the kingdom.

Both are gifts

Paul writes, “I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another” (1 Corinthians 7:7). His wish is pastoral, not a command. He uses the word for a gift of grace, and he applies it to both singleness and marriage. Neither is superior in every circumstance, and both need God’s grace to be lived well.

Single people tempted to feel they have the lesser gift should read this carefully. Paul, who had more gospel impact than almost anyone, saw his singleness as a gift that freed him for that impact. Married people tempted to think single people incomplete should read it equally carefully. Completeness is found in Christ, not in a spouse.

Paul’s contentment

Writing from prison, Paul said, “I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content” (Philippians 4:11). His singleness was part of his circumstances. He did not treat it as a tragedy, but as a freedom: to be beaten for the gospel without a wife and children left behind, to travel without a family’s schedule, to pour himself out for the churches with undivided attention. His contentment was not resignation. It was the freedom of someone whose deepest satisfaction was in Christ.

Marriage honoured

At the same time, Scripture honours marriage throughout, as a creation gift, a gospel sign and a profound good. “Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4). That command is for everyone, single people included. Single believers honour marriage by celebrating their married friends, by refusing cynicism about it, and by keeping sexual union for its proper place. Married believers honour it by faithfulness, and by refusing adultery and pornography. Purity is not only a concern before marriage. It is a calling for life.

And a single person who longs to marry is not spiritually immature. They are expressing a good, God-given desire for the companionship and union that God himself designed.

Not carried into the next age

Jesus taught that “in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30). Marriage is glorious and good for this age, but it is not carried into the next. That is not bad news for married people. It means the best is yet to come: the union to which their marriage points is far more satisfying than anything they have known.

And it is real good news for single people. The thing they have not experienced in this life is not the best thing. The best thing is what no one has yet fully experienced, and they will receive it in exactly the same measure as every married person who ever lived.

The church as family

Jesus redefined family around himself. Looking at those around him, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother” (Mark 3:34–35). The early church spoke as a family: brothers and sisters, mothers and fathers in the faith. A church that truly lives as family, where single people are not isolated and married couples are not self-sufficient, shows the world the kingdom’s new kind of belonging.

From Cana to the marriage supper

Jesus’ first sign was at a wedding in Cana. He supplied the wine of gladness, and so “manifested his glory” (John 2:11). And the final celebration of his reign will also be a wedding. “Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7).

This is where every marriage and every single life is heading. The bride, the church, bought with Christ’s blood and washed by his word, is ready. Every marriage that pointed to this, every single life lived for this, every promise kept in hardship and every costly forgiveness, has been preparation for that day. “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). The finest wedding in history will pale beside it, and everyone who is in Christ will be there.

For reflection

Whether you are married or single, how does the marriage supper of the Lamb shape the way you see your present calling? How could your church become more truly a family for both?
